bio: Jess Whittlestone is a Senior Adviser on AI Policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR), a UK think tank focused on extreme risks, where she was Head (later Director) of AI Policy from 2022, leading the development of and advocacy for CLTR's AI recommendations in senior UK policy circles, including evidence to Parliament on AI governance and compute. Before CLTR she was a Senior Research Fellow and Deputy Director of the AI: Futures and Responsibility Programme at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk at Cambridge. With Jack Clark she wrote 'Why and How Governments Should Monitor AI Development' (2021), an early blueprint for state capacity to measure AI capabilities that anticipated government AI safety institutes. She holds a PhD in Behavioural Science from Warwick and a master's in Mathematics and Philosophy from Oxford, and is a member of the CNAS AI Governance Forum.

He holds a bachelor's degree in Philosophy, Politics and Economics from the University of Oxford and a master's degree from Johns Hopkins' School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS). He speaks Dutch, English and Arabic and shares regular video updates on AI policy. FLI's policy work during his tenure includes the AI Safety Index, which grades frontier AI developers on their safety practices.

bio: Risto Uuk is Head of European Policy and Research at the Future of Life Institute, where he contributed to shaping the general-purpose AI and systemic-risk provisions of the EU AI Act. He is a PhD researcher at KU Leuven, a member of Estonia's government AI advisory board under the Prime Minister, and co-author of the forthcoming book 'The AI Endgame' (Wiley). He leads the EU AI Act Newsletter, which has more than 50,000 subscribers. Previously he worked at the World Economic Forum on positive AI economic futures and conducted research for the European Commission on trustworthy AI. His research includes 'A Taxonomy of Systemic Risks from General-Purpose AI' (2024), which systematised the systemic risks the AI Act requires providers to assess. He holds a master's in Philosophy and Public Policy from the London School of Economics and a bachelor's from Tallinn University.

bio: Emilia Javorsky, MD, MPH, is the Director of the Futures Program at the Future of Life Institute, where she leads work on imagining and architecting futures that realise the benefits of emerging technology while mitigating its risks. By training she is a physician-scientist and entrepreneur who has worked on inventing, developing and translating medical technologies, and she is a scientist and mentor at the Wyss Institute at Harvard. She has authored over a dozen publications and is an inventor on several patents. Previously she was a Fulbright-Schuman scholar to the European Union, a Young Pioneer of the World Frontiers Forum, a Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree and a Global Shaper of the World Economic Forum. She describes herself as passionate about ensuring that emerging technologies are deployed safely, ethically and for the betterment of humanity.

bio: Haydn Belfield was a Research Associate and Academic Project Manager at the University of Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER) from January 2017 to March 2025 and remains a Research Affiliate; he is also an Associate Fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. During that time CSER tripled in size and he advised the UK, US and Singaporean governments, the EU, UN and OECD, and leading technology companies. He has more than 30 publications on climate change, pandemics and societal collapse, but most of his work concerns the security implications of AI, including 'The Malicious Use of AI: Forecasting, Prevention, and Mitigation' (2018), 'Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims' (2020) and 'Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence' (2024). Earlier he worked in UK politics as senior parliamentary researcher to a Shadow Cabinet MP. He studied PPE and politics at Oxford, where he is a DPhil candidate in International Relations.

bio: Shahar Avin is an Assistant Research Professor at the University of Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk. His research examines the challenges and opportunities in implementing risk-mitigation strategies, particularly where there is high uncertainty and heterogeneous or conflicting interests and incentives. Mixing anthropological methods and agent-based modelling, he works with CSER colleagues and the wider existential-risk community to identify and design opportunities for impact. He was a co-author of the landmark 2018 report 'The Malicious Use of Artificial Intelligence' and of 'Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims' (2020), and co-authored CLTR's 2022 evidence to the UK Future of Compute Review. He completed his doctoral thesis on the rational allocation of public resources to scientific research at Cambridge's Department of History and Philosophy of Science, and previously worked as a software engineer.

Concordia publishes the annual 'State of AI Safety in China' reports and participates in Chinese national AI safety standards committees. He co-edited the book 'Global Perspective on AI Governance' and graduated from the University of Hong Kong.

Under his direction SaferAI developed ratings of the risk-management maturity of frontier AI companies, featured in TIME, and a frontier AI risk-management framework that bridges current AI practices with established risk-management disciplines. He has been a technical expert in the ISO/IEC and CEN-CENELEC standardisation bodies working on AI risk-management standards for large language models, and is a member of the OECD AI expert network on AI risk and accountability. He previously co-founded EffiSciences, which trained hundreds of French students in AI safety, and worked on an LLM startup.

bio: Sneha Revanur is an American activist and the founder and president of Encode (formerly Encode Justice), a youth-led organisation advocating for the regulation of artificial intelligence. She created Encode in July 2020 while a high-school sophomore in San Jose, on the belief that young people — who will live longest with the consequences of AI — deserve a voice in how it is governed. Encode co-sponsored California's SB 1047 and sponsored SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, which became the first US frontier-AI safety law in 2025. She studied Symbolic Systems at Stanford and was the youngest person named to TIME's inaugural list of the 100 most influential people in AI; Politico has called her 'the Greta Thunberg of AI'. In 2026 she discussed on the 80,000 Hours podcast how a small team helped pass AI safety legislation.

His policy work also covers New York's RAISE Act and opposition to federal preemption of state AI law. He holds a JD and a Master's in Public Policy from Stanford, is a Johns Hopkins Emerging Leaders in Biosecurity Fellow, and previously worked at the Center for AI Safety Action Fund and the US Senate Judiciary Committee.

bio: Rebecca Finlay is CEO of the Partnership on AI (PAI), a global nonprofit bringing together more than 100 academic, civil-society, industry and media partners to ensure AI advances positive outcomes for people and society. She joined PAI's board in early 2020, became acting executive director in 2021 and was appointed CEO in October 2021. Previously she was Vice President of Engagement and Public Policy at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR), where she founded the AI & Society program in 2017 — one of the first international multistakeholder initiatives on AI's societal impact — and led CIFAR's partnerships with governments. Under her leadership PAI published its Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment. She is a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, sits on advisory bodies in Canada, France and the US, spoke at the UK AI Safety Summit, and holds degrees from McGill and Cambridge.

bio: Heidy Khlaaf is Chief AI Scientist at the AI Now Institute, focusing on the assessment and safety of AI in defence and national security, including autonomous weapons and decision-support systems. She specialises in the evaluation, specification and verification of complex or autonomous software in safety-critical systems, having led system safety audits under standards such as IEC 61508 and DO-178C for systems ranging from UAVs to nuclear power plants. She helped establish the field of AI safety engineering and is known for leading the safety evaluation of Codex at OpenAI, developing a methodology that MIT Technology Review says has since been adopted by AI labs worldwide. At Trail of Bits she founded the AI/ML assurance practice and led cyber evaluations with the UK AI Safety Institute. She has criticised the 'arms race' narrative used to justify rapid military AI adoption. She holds a PhD in formal verification from UCL and was named to the TIME100 AI 2025 list and MIT Technology Review's 35 Under 35.

bio: Lucilla Sioli is the Director of the European AI Office within the European Commission's Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT). The AI Office, set up within the Commission in 2024, is responsible for implementing the AI Act — including the obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk — and oversaw the drafting of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice published in July 2025. She is responsible for coordinating the European AI strategy and its governance, including the AI Continent Action Plan and the Apply AI strategy, international collaboration on AI and AI for good, and R&D&I in AI and key sectors such as healthcare, robotics and advanced manufacturing. Before the AI Office she was Director for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Industry, covering policy including the AI Act and Chips Act. She holds PhDs in economics from the University of Southampton and the Catholic University of Milan and has been a Commission civil servant since 1997.

bio: Kim Myuhng-joo (also written Myuhng Joo Kim) is the inaugural director of the Korea AI Safety Institute, which launched in Pangyo in November 2024 as a follow-up to the AI Seoul Summit; his three-year term runs to November 2027. A security expert with bachelor's, master's and PhD degrees in computer science and engineering from Seoul National University, he was a professor of information security at Seoul Women's University and has led the Right AI with Security & Ethics (RAISE) Research Center since 2019. A long-time advocate of digital ethics, he helped found the Korea Society of Internet Ethics, chaired the AI Ethics Policy Forum, introduced the 'Seoul PACT' (Publicness, Accountability, Controllability, Transparency) — described as Korea's first AI ethics declaration — and, as a government-appointed expert to the Global Partnership on AI, contributed to Korea's AI Basic Act. He has framed the institute as supporting Korean AI firms to minimise risks rather than acting as a regulator.

bio: Vivek Hebbar is a member of technical staff at Redwood Research working on AI control and misalignment science. bio: Bronson Schoen is a member of technical staff at Apollo Research, which studies scheming — AI systems covertly pursuing misaligned goals — and how to evaluate and mitigate it. His X profile lists earlier engineering roles at NVIDIA and Apple. He was a co-first author of 'Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming' (December 2024), Apollo's influential evaluation showing that frontier models would disable oversight, sandbag or fake alignment when given in-context goals, where he provided engineering support. He then led the Apollo side of a 2025 collaboration with OpenAI, 'Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training', contributing evaluations, analysis and experiments across 180+ out-of-distribution environments. The study found that anti-scheming training sharply reduced covert actions (for example from 8.7% to 0.3% for one model) but did not eliminate them, and that models' growing awareness of being evaluated complicates interpreting such results.

bio: Tony Tong Wang is a PhD candidate at MIT and a member of technical staff at the US government's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). His research centres on adversarial robustness, which he sees as closely tied to safety because safe systems need acceptable worst-case performance. As lead author of 'Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs' (ICML 2023), written with FAR.AI researchers, he showed that an adversarial agent could reliably defeat KataGo, a superhuman Go program, by tricking it into blunders rather than by playing well — an exploit simple enough that human amateurs could replicate it. He argues that phenomena like jailbreaks show RLHF instils heuristics rather than changing a model's 'core' values, and he has studied robustness in toy settings and in vision as a stepping stone to robustness against unrestricted adversaries.

bio: Kevin Meng is a founding member of Transluce, the independent nonprofit lab building open tools for understanding and overseeing AI systems, where he builds tools to accelerate open science on AI agent behavior. Working with David Bau, Alex Andonian and Yonatan Belinkov, he developed causal tracing, a technique for locating where GPT models store factual associations, and ROME (Rank-One Model Editing), which edits individual facts directly into model weights ('Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT', NeurIPS 2022). The follow-up MEMIT ('Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer', ICLR 2023) scaled editing to thousands of memories at once in GPT-J and GPT-NeoX. These papers became foundational in mechanistic interpretability and knowledge editing. He has also shown that Apple's NeuralHash is approximately linear, enabling black-box attacks, and earlier adversarially trained a claim-spotting model deployed on the ClaimBuster fact-checking platform.

Lakera became one of the leading AI-native security platforms for LLM and agent applications, with products such as Lakera Guard for runtime protection and Lakera Red for pre-deployment assessments, and it built Gandalf, a viral game in which players try to trick an LLM into revealing a password — creating one of the world's largest crowdsourced red-teaming datasets, analysed in the paper 'Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs'. bio: Andy Arditi is an interpretability researcher and PhD student in David Bau's lab at Northeastern University. After studying computer science and mathematics at Columbia, working as a software engineer at Microsoft and then on zero-knowledge cryptography at the startup Scroll, he shifted to AI interpretability in August 2023. Working independently and as a MATS researcher, with co-authors including Neel Nanda, he was lead author of 'Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction' (NeurIPS 2024), which showed across 13 open chat models up to 72B parameters that refusal is controlled by a single residual-stream direction: ablating it disables refusal and adding it induces refusal. The accompanying weight-orthogonalisation trick became widely used to strip safeguards from open-weight models ('abliteration'), sharpening debates about open-model safety. As an Anthropic AI Safety Research Fellow he co-authored 'Persona Vectors' (2025). He also wrote with Bilal Chughtai that unlearning via RMU is mostly shallow.

bio: Jeremy Schlatter is a software engineer with a computer science degree from Washington University in St. Louis. He worked at Google and Mailgun before joining OpenAI in late 2016, where he built parts of OpenAI Universe's infrastructure and contributed to the Dota 2 bot; he is a co-author of 'Dota 2 with Large Scale Deep Reinforcement Learning.' I have worked in AI for a decade. quotes.text:
OpenAI has said that humans should remain in control of AI development, and that decisions about the pace of progress should be made through democratic processes rather than left to individual labs. I strongly agree.

Progress is already moving very quickly. By default, competitive pressure rewards whichever company or country is willing to move fastest and accept the most risk. Recursive self-improvement could dramatically accelerate those dynamics, potentially beyond our collective ability to understand progress, assess risks, and maintain meaningful human oversight.

We should start with stronger domestic transparency about frontier training, internal deployment, the pace of progress, and the risks and safeguards associated with increasingly capable systems. Democratic decisions are impossible if the public and policymakers don’t have the information they need to make them.

But transparency alone won’t solve an international race. We also need to build the technical and governance capacity for credible, verifiable international coordination. Maybe we never need to use it. But with many experts considering an intelligence explosion plausible within the next two years, I think it's urgent that we start building this capacity now.
quotes.context: Pacing the Frontier statement, July 2026

quotes.text:
I support keeping humanity in control of frontier AI, but we need to be thoughtful about how we do it.

If governance only applies to public models, we risk pushing the most advanced capabilities into private or specialized systems, beyond independent scrutiny and accessible only to a select few. That could concentrate power without meaningfully reducing risk.

Effective oversight must be measurable, verifiable, and applicable across public and private development, while protecting sensitive data. Otherwise, we may slow access without slowing the frontier.

bio: Daniel P. (Danny) Sawyer is a Senior Research Scientist at Google DeepMind in the San Francisco Bay Area, working on agentic exploration in text and embodied environments. He was part of the team behind SIMA, the generalist agent that follows natural-language instructions across commercial 3D games such as No Man's Sky and Valheim, and its Gemini-based successor SIMA 2 (2025). Before DeepMind he worked at Vicarious and earned a PhD in bioengineering at Caltech in Mikhail Shapiro's lab, on ultrasound imaging of gene expression.
